missingAiRole.title: The mathlib4 repository is created as the Lean 4 mathematics library of the Lean prover community
missingAiRole.summary: On 2021-05-09 the leanprover-community organization created the leanprover-community/mathlib4 repository, described as 'The math library of Lean 4', giving the community's formal mathematics library a dedicated home in the Lean 4 ecosystem (Apache-2.0, written in Lean).

missingAiRole.title: SVAMP: Are NLP Models really able to Solve Simple Math Word Problems?
missingAiRole.summary: A NAACL 2021 paper showing that math word problem solvers rely on shallow heuristics — models without access to the question, or treating problems as bag-of-words, still solve a large fraction of existing benchmarks — and introducing SVAMP, a challenge set built by applying carefully chosen variations to examples from existing datasets.

missingAiRole.title: Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset
missingAiRole.summary: A dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems (AMC/AIME-style and beyond), each with a full step-by-step solution, organized by subject and by difficulty levels 1–5.

missingAiRole.summary: The authors present a formal proof in Lean of probably approximately correct (PAC) learnability for decision stumps, a classic result in machine learning theory bounding the error probability of a simple classifier. missingAiRole.summary: The paper presents a new approach to automated theorem proving in which polynomial-cost procedures that recognize sentences belonging to a given theory are generated directly from a set of axioms of Truncated Predicate Calculus, a subset of standard predicate calculus. missingAiRole.summary: The paper presents a formalization of forcing via Boolean-valued models in the Lean 3 theorem prover. missingAiRole.title: HOList: a learning environment and benchmark for HOL Light
missingAiRole.summary: Bansal, Loos, Rabe, Szegedy and Wilcox released HOList, a HOL Light environment and benchmark for learning-guided higher-order theorem proving.

missingAiRole.title: Formal Proofs of Tarjan's Algorithm in Why3, Coq, and Isabelle
missingAiRole.summary: The paper presents a formal proof of correctness for Tarjan's algorithm, a non-trivial algorithm from graph theory, developed independently in three proof assistants: Why3, Coq, and Isabelle. missingAiRole.summary: This work extends the mathlib library of Lean with foundations of computability theory, using primitive recursive functions and partial recursive functions as the main objects. missingAiRole.summary: This paper compares two widely used automated theorem proving tools, Isabelle/HOL and Coq, with respect to expressiveness, limitations, and usability. missingAiRole.title: Proof Simplification and Automated Theorem Proving
missingAiRole.summary: This paper describes a technique for simplifying proofs that automated theorem provers first generate, which are typically far from optimal by any measure of simplicity. missingAiRole.title: GamePad: a learning environment for theorem proving
missingAiRole.summary: Huang, Dhariwal, Song and Sutskever introduced GamePad, a Coq-based environment that exposes proof states and tactics to reinforcement-learning agents.

missingAiRole.summary: The paper describes the Natural Deduction Assistant (NaDeA) and its interfaces with the Isabelle proof assistant. missingAiRole.summary: This work formalizes Matiyasevič's theorem in the Lean theorem prover, showing that the power function is Diophantine. missingAiRole.title: mathlib: a unified mathematical library for Lean
missingAiRole.summary: The leanprover-community/mathlib repository was created on 2017-07-21, giving Lean 3 a community-maintained library of formal mathematics that grew into the standard corpus for Lean-based proving and AI4Math.

missingAiRole.title: HolStep: a machine-learning dataset for HOL Light theorem proving
missingAiRole.summary: Kaliszyk, Chollet and Szegedy released HolStep, a dataset of HOL Light proof steps annotated as useful or not, to support learning-guided theorem proving.

missingAiRole.title: A formal proof of the Kepler conjecture completes the Flyspeck project
missingAiRole.summary: Hales and collaborators published a formal proof of the Kepler conjecture in HOL Light and Isabelle, completing the Flyspeck project; the 2015 paper describes the formalization and its verification.

missingAiRole.title: Lean's theorem prover repository goes public
missingAiRole.summary: On 2013-07-17 the leanprover/lean3 repository was created, making Leonardo de Moura's Lean theorem prover available as an open project; Lean was described at CADE 2015 as a dependently typed prover aimed at verification and mathematics.

missingAiRole.title: A machine-checked proof of the Odd Order Theorem in Coq
missingAiRole.summary: Gonthier and collaborators completed a Coq formalization of the Feit–Thompson Odd Order Theorem, presented at ITP 2012, covering the whole proof of a landmark group-theory result.

missingAiRole.title: Sledgehammer brings strong automation into everyday Isabelle proofs
missingAiRole.summary: Böhme and Nipkow's 2010 ITP paper evaluated Sledgehammer, Isabelle's bridge from interactive goals to external ATPs, showing that relevance filtering and parallel provers made one-click automation effective on Isabelle proof obligations.

missingAiRole.title: MPTP turns the Mizar library into a large-theory benchmark for ATP
missingAiRole.summary: Josef Urban's MPTP translated the Mizar Mathematical Library into TPTP problems and paired it with machine-learned premise selection, giving automated theorem provers a large, noisy theory to reason in; the Journal of Automated Reasoning paper reported the design and first experiments in 2004.

missingAiRole.title: CASC: the CADE ATP System Competition
missingAiRole.summary: The first CADE ATP System Competition was held at CADE-13 in 1996, evaluating automated theorem provers on TPTP problems under common hardware and time limits.

missingAiRole.title: The QED Manifesto calls for a computer-checked corpus of all mathematics
missingAiRole.summary: The 1994 QED Manifesto argued for a long-term project to formalize mathematics in machine-checkable form and to build a shared library of checked proofs.

missingAiRole.title: Isabelle: a generic theorem prover in the LCF tradition
missingAiRole.summary: Paulson's 1989 Journal of Automated Reasoning paper described Isabelle, a generic proof assistant in which object logics are embedded as theories and proofs are constructed with tactics.

missingAiRole.title: HOL88 brings the HOL system to a wider user community
missingAiRole.summary: HOL88, developed by Gordon and Melham at Cambridge, was a widely distributed version of the HOL proof assistant that made the HOL approach available beyond the original implementation.

missingAiRole.title: HOL: a proof-generating system for higher-order logic
missingAiRole.summary: Mike Gordon's 1987 technical report described HOL, a proof-generating system for higher-order logic built in the LCF style and aimed at hardware verification.

missingAiRole.title: Nuprl implements number theory in a constructive type theory
missingAiRole.summary: Howe's 1986 paper reported an experiment implementing number theory in Nuprl, the constructive type-theory proof system developed at Cornell by Constable and colleagues.

missingAiRole.title: Coq is started at Inria as an implementation of the Calculus of Constructions
missingAiRole.summary: The Coq proof assistant was started in 1984 by Gérard Huet and Thierry Coquand; version 1 appeared in 1985, and later versions added universes, automation, extraction and inductive types, as recorded in the Rocq reference manual's history.

missingAiRole.title: Maple offers portable interactive symbolic computation
missingAiRole.summary: The Maple symbolic computation system, described by Char, Geddes and Gonnet in 1983, provided interactive symbolic algebra and calculus with a focus on efficiency and portability.

missingAiRole.title: Edinburgh LCF turns the LCF idea into a usable proof assistant
missingAiRole.summary: The 1979 Edinburgh LCF system, documented by Gordon, Milner and Wadsworth, implemented a programmable proof assistant for a logic of computable functions with a small kernel, tactics and the ML metalanguage.

missingAiRole.title: Wu's method turns elementary geometry into polynomial algebra
missingAiRole.summary: Wu Wen-tsün's algebraic method (1977) reduced elementary geometry theorems to polynomial equations and used characteristic sets to decide them, giving a mechanical procedure that proved large classes of geometry theorems.

missingAiRole.title: LCF introduces machine-checked proofs with tactics and the ML metalanguage
missingAiRole.summary: Robin Milner's 1972 LCF system implemented Scott's logic for computable functions and introduced the tactic style of interactive proof, in which proofs are constructed by programs written in ML.

missingAiRole.title: MACSYMA brings large-scale symbolic algebra to interactive computing
missingAiRole.summary: MACSYMA, reported by Martin and Fateman at SYMSAC 1971, integrated symbolic algebra, simplification, calculus and linear algebra into an interactive system developed at MIT's Project MAC.

missingAiRole.title: de Bruijn's Automath language makes mechanical proof checking a design goal
missingAiRole.summary: N. G. de Bruijn's Automath (1968) introduced a formal language in which mathematical statements and proofs are written so that a machine can check them, an early type-theoretic foundation for proof assistants.

missingAiRole.title: Robinson's resolution principle gives automated theorem proving a single inference rule
missingAiRole.summary: J. A. Robinson's 1965 Journal of the ACM paper introduced resolution, a single inference rule for first-order logic based on unification and refutation, which became the foundation of most later automated theorem provers.
